verses.note: The verb for Abel's blood crying out is the same verb Scripture uses for the cry of the powerless whom God hears. The first victim of violence becomes the first voice God attends to on behalf of someone who could not defend himself.
Israel's law later commands that a runaway slave not be returned to a master or oppressed (Deuteronomy 23:15-16). Hagar's story shows why such a law was needed, even in Abram's own house.
The chosen family is marked by righteousness and justice, the very things absent from Sodom (Ezekiel 16:49). The contrast between Abraham's household and Sodom is set up in God's own words.

The law repeatedly names the widow among those God defends (Exodus 22:22, Deuteronomy 10:18). Judah's delay leaves Tamar with neither support nor freedom, and the rest of the chapter turns on the question of who will do right by her.
Joseph's revised plan provides for the hungry households back in Canaan, not only for the men in front of him. Even his testing is bent toward feeding the vulnerable.
